A lighthouse keeper or lightkeeper is the person responsible for tending and caring for a lighthouse, particularly the light and lens in the days when oil lamps and clockwork mechanisms were used.[1] Lighthouse keepers were sometimes referred to as "wickies" because of their job trimming the wicks.

Keepers were needed to trim wicks, replenish fuel, wind clockworks and perform maintenance tasks such as cleaning lenses and windows.[2][3] Remote lighthouses were often staffed by several keepers who worked in shifts through the night.

History

[edit]

The earliest keepers tended open coal fires on towers along the Mediterranean coast, a job that demanded constant attention during storms and long winter nights.[4]

By the nineteenth century, keepers were usually employed by national lighthouse authorities, which issued strict rules about logbooks, uniforms and the hours at which the light had to be lit.[citation needed] Families often lived at the station and shared the work.

Automation

[edit]

Electrification and automatic lamp changers gradually removed the need for resident keepers during the twentieth century, and most stations around the world are now monitored remotely.[5]

Duties

[edit]

A keeper's routine typically included lighting the lamp at sunset, keeping watch through the night, and extinguishing it at sunrise, followed by cleaning the lens and recording the weather.

  • Polishing the brass fittings and the glass prisms of the lens.
  • Sounding the fog signal whenever visibility dropped.

In emergencies, keepers also took part in rescues of shipwrecked sailors, and some became famous for their bravery in launching small boats into heavy seas.[6]
